nameStory: The "oxeye" name comes from the flower's resemblance to a large, bright eye - specifically that of an ox or bull. The golden-yellow center surrounded by white petals does look remarkably like a wide-open eye gazing up from the meadow. Some folks also call it "dog daisy," though no one's quite sure why our canine friends got dragged into the naming!
description: Oxeye daisy is a cheerful perennial wildflower that looks like the classic daisy most people picture when they think "daisy." It grows 1-3 feet tall with bright white petals radiating around a golden-yellow center, creating flowers about 2 inches across. The plant forms colonies through underground stems, often creating patches of dozens of these sunny faces nodding in fields and roadsides. It's actually a European native that has made itself thoroughly at home across New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic daisy appearance with 15-30 white petals (actually ray flowers) surrounding a bright golden-yellow center that feels slightly bumpy to the touch and smells faintly sweet

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Dark green leaves that feel somewhat thick and leathery, with deeply toothed or lobed edges that look like they've been cut with pinking shears

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in patches or colonies with multiple stems rising from the ground, each topped with a single flower that nods gently in the breeze

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, upright stems that feel firm and slightly ridged when you run your finger along them, usually unbranched until near the top

habitat: Look for oxeye daisies in sunny, open areas like fields, meadows, roadsides, and abandoned lots throughout New England. They prefer well-drained soils and don't mind poor or disturbed ground. You'll often find them mixed with other non-native wildflowers like Queen Anne's lace and chicory in old farm fields and along rural roads.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as low rosettes, with the characteristic toothed foliage becoming recognizable by late spring before flower stalks appear.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from June through August, when the distinctive white and yellow flowers are most abundant and easiest to spot.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and plants begin setting seed, with some late blooms possible into early fall if conditions are favorable.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving little trace above ground until spring growth resumes from the root system.

funFact: Despite being called a single "flower," what you're looking at is actually a flower head made up of dozens of tiny individual flowers - the white "petals" are each complete flowers themselves, while the yellow center contains up to 750 microscopic tube-shaped flowers all packed together!
confusionNotes: Often confused with Shasta daisies in gardens, but oxeye daisies are smaller, have more deeply cut leaves, and grow wild rather than being planted. The leaves are the giveaway - oxeye daisy leaves look much more jagged and "wild" compared to Shasta daisy's smoother, less divided foliage.
contextualKnowledge: This European immigrant has been in North America so long that many people assume it's native - it was likely brought by early colonists, possibly as a medicinal herb. In some states it's actually considered a noxious weed because it can take over pastures, but in New England it's generally just part of the naturalized landscape.
compareHints: Oxeye daisy is much smaller than its relative max chrysanthemum (Shasta daisy), with flowers typically 2 inches across versus 3-4 inches. The leaves are also more deeply divided and darker green than the Shasta daisy's broader, less-cut foliage. Oxeye daisy also spreads more aggressively and naturalizes readily, while Shasta daisies tend to stay put in garden settings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Max chrysanthemum is basically the big brother of oxeye daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare) - same family resemblance but supersized.
